strengths: Clean and principled formalization of active perception as a POMDP that unifies a differentiable prediction loss with a standard RL reward, yielding a clear policy-gradient decomposition (Eq. 3) that is intuitive and well-derived.

Two concrete instantiations (APPLE-SAC and APPLE-CrossQ) are provided, along with an ablation with a PPO-based variant, giving insight into the effect of off-policy vs on-policy learning for active perception.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning classification, regression, and pose-estimation tasks (MHSB, CircleSquare, TactileMNIST, TactileMNISTVolume, Toolbox), with 5 seeds per configuration and a sensible random-policy baseline (APPLE-RND) that helps isolate the contribution of active exploration.

Clear demonstration that the proposed off-policy methods vastly outperform the on-policy HAM baseline in sample efficiency, with a plausible explanation (sample reuse) supported by additional PPO-based experiments in the appendix.
Good attention to reproducibility: detailed hyperparameter search procedure (HEBO), full appendix with environment specifics, GPU/compute details, and a promise to release code.
The shared transformer backbone architecture for jointly processing perception and control inputs is a sensible design choice that is empirically justified (shared vs separate embeddings).
weaknesses: Despite the framing as a "general" active perception framework, all experiments are restricted to the tactile domain and largely drawn from a single benchmark suite (Schneider et al. 2025); no experiments in vision-based or other modalities are shown despite motivating discussion of vision-based active perception in the introduction, making the generality claim not fully substantiated.

The RL reward r(h_t, a_t) is only used as a minor L2 action-magnitude penalty across all tasks, so the framework's claimed ability to incorporate arbitrary task-specific RL rewards alongside the prediction loss is not actually tested empirically.

Baseline comparison is limited to HAM (2020), a relatively old on-policy method; more recent RL-based tactile active perception approaches mentioned in related work (e.g., TANDEM, ActExplore, DQN-based shape reconstruction) are not empirically compared, leaving open whether APPLE's gains are simply due to using a modern off-policy algorithm rather than a genuinely novel formulation.

Results on the Toolbox task show APPLE-SAC failing to clearly beat the random baseline when hyperparameters are not retuned, which somewhat undercuts the claimed robustness/generality of the framework and suggests sensitivity to hyperparameter transfer.

Sample efficiency remains poor (up to 5-10M environment steps for relatively simple simulated tasks), which is acknowledged as a limitation but limits practical significance and real-world applicability, and no real-robot experiments are included.

The core theoretical contribution (decomposing the RL objective into a policy gradient term plus a supervised prediction-loss gradient term) is a fairly direct consequence of the problem setup and standard REINFORCE-style derivations, so the algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental relative to combining existing SAC/CrossQ with a supervised loss term.

Variance across seeds is fairly high in several plots (e.g., TactileMNISTVolume, Toolbox), and no statistical significance testing is reported to support claims of one method being better than another.

strengths: Principled and clean derivation of the active perception objective as a POMDP where the gradient decomposes cleanly into a policy-gradient term and a supervised prediction-loss gradient term (Eq. 3), giving a well-motivated theoretical basis for combining RL and supervised learning.

Two concrete, easy-to-implement instantiations (APPLE-SAC and APPLE-CrossQ) built on established off-policy actor-critic algorithms, with clear engineering choices (shared transformer backbone, ViT tactile encoder, dynamic reward recomputation for the Bellman residual).

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation spanning classification (MHSB, CircleSquare, TactileMNIST, CIFAR10), regression (TactileMNISTVolume), and pose estimation (Toolbox), demonstrating the framework is not hard-coded to a single task type.

Extensive and informative ablation studies in the appendix (LSTM vs. transformer backbone, pure-RL vs. supervised-loss-augmented objective, sparse-reward setting, downstream-task-conditioned reward, PPO vs. off-policy variants), which substantially strengthen the empirical support for the paper's core design choices.

Clear demonstration that on-policy methods (HAM, PPO variants) struggle with sample efficiency and even fail to beat random guessing on some tasks, providing a reasonably convincing argument for the off-policy design choice.

Qualitative visualizations of learned exploration strategies (e.g., gradient-following in CircleSquare, circular search + sliding-along-handle in Toolbox) that provide intuitive, interpretable evidence the policies are meaningfully non-random.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameter search procedure (HEBO), architecture/implementation details, and an LLM usage disclosure.
weaknesses: All experiments are purely in simulation; despite motivating the work heavily around real-world robotic tactile exploration, there is no real-robot validation, and the discussion itself flags sim-to-real transfer of soft-gel tactile sensors as an unresolved, nontrivial challenge.

The generality claim is somewhat overstated: aside from CircleSquare/CIFAR10 toy tasks, the core benchmarks are all drawn from a single tactile benchmark suite (Schneider et al., 2025) with a shared sensor (GelSight Mini) and similar action/observation structure, so true cross-domain or cross-modality generality (e.g., vision-only or multi-modal active perception) is not demonstrated.

The main baseline (HAM) is a relatively old REINFORCE-based method not designed for the newer benchmark tasks and requiring architecture modifications (removing/adding vision encoders) for fair comparison; more recent and stronger active tactile perception baselines (e.g., TANDEM/PPO, ActExplore, DQN-based shape reconstruction) mentioned in related work are not empirically compared against, making the 'general SOTA framework' claim less convincingly supported.

Sample efficiency remains poor (millions of environment steps, tens of hours per run), which the authors acknowledge, but this significantly undercuts practical applicability claims and is not mitigated with any concrete efficiency improvements (e.g., pretrained encoders) in this work.

APPLE-SAC's noticeably weaker/unstable performance on the untuned Toolbox task suggests residual hyperparameter sensitivity, partially undermining the 'general framework requiring minimal task-specific tuning' narrative, even though APPLE-CrossQ fares better.

Results are reported only as mean ± std over 5 seeds without formal statistical significance testing, and some comparisons (e.g., MHSB task) are acknowledged by the authors themselves to be somewhat trivial/easy given the task's small discretized observation space, weakening the strength of certain headline comparisons.

The paper's scope explicitly excludes active perception in service of a downstream task (only a small proof-of-concept ablation in the appendix addresses this), which is arguably the more practically relevant and harder setting for real robotic applications.
